blocks.text: The OpenAI engineer who was charged this week with planting a secret recording device at the artificial intelligence company recently said he helped advise government agencies in Saudi Arabia on technology, and was listed as a partner at a venture capital firm alongside a member of the Saudi royal family.

In an Arabic podcast interview last month, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, said he and other Saudi tech professionals in Silicon Valley had formed a group that advised Saudi organizations, including the kingdom’s social insurance agency. Separately, RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm in Riyadh, the Saudi capital, lists Mr. Alfozan as a venture partner on its website, along with Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud.

Mr. Alfozan has a long history in Silicon Valley. He was an engineer at Meta before joining a start-up that went through Y Combinator, the Silicon Valley start-up accelerator. He gained permanent residency status in the United States in 2020, according to court documents, and was hired by OpenAI in July 2025.

Details about Mr. Alfozan are emerging after OpenAI disclosed on Tuesday that it had discovered a hidden recording device in a conference room in one of its San Francisco buildings. The company said it had traced the device to Mr. Alfozan, who was arrested by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and charged with trying to secretly record conversations using an electronic device.

The incident has fueled concerns about the security of leading A.I. labs like OpenAI, which create advanced A.I. models that are among the most closely guarded secrets in the U.S. technology industry. Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, said that what had happened at OpenAI underscored how winning the A.I. race “is a national security prerogative.”

OpenAI said Mr. Alfozan did not appear to have inappropriately obtained or extracted sensitive information about its technology or customers. But the cloak-and-dagger details of the case have gained attention in Silicon Valley and in law enforcement and national security circles.
